doc.title: Harry Allen interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 13, 1997

title: 'Young lions' hype and avoiding rock gigs
summary: Dislikes industry picking stars by look; never played rock, only some Top 40 at weddings.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: What do you think about the hype, the press that the “young lions” get? Have you ever been called a “young lion” in the press?

I don’t think so. I think it’s too bad — it’s great for them and their careers obviously. It’s too bad in a way because I feel that somebody in an office somewhere is making the decision as to who is going to be able to make it, whereas I gather that years ago it was more like the best guys were the ones who made it. And today it’s, oh well, you are the right look, you are the right this, well we’re going to put the money behind you. And obviously that’s not the way to do it if you’re going to get the best musical results. But it’s certainly great for those individuals. That’s wonderful for them.
When you were coming up through high school and then in college, did you play gigs that were far astray from what you really wanted to do? Did you ever get into the rock & roll scene?
No. No, I never did. The farthest I’ve ever gotten is playing some weddings where they wanted jazz and having to play some Top 40 tune or two.
Come on. Did you ever play “Tequila?”
I probably have played “Tequila” once or twice at one of those jobs.
